---
title: "Conceptual Model"
subtitle: "The full specification of the TimeToAlign! cross-domain timeline model"
toc-depth: 4
---

This page presents the complete conceptual model underlying TimeToAlign!.
The accompanying [TISMIR manuscript](https://anonymous.example.com) introduces
these concepts through five worked examples; this page serves as the
authoritative reference for formal definitions and visual conventions.

The model is organised in six layers, each building on the previous:

1. [**Foundations**](#foundations): Domains, timelines, coordinates, instants, events
2. [**Flow control**](#flow-control): Contiguity, breaks, jumps
3. [**Conversion maps**](#conversion-maps): Coordinate transformations
4. [**Nested timelines**](#nested-timelines): Children, segments, timestamps
5. [**Regions and derivative timelines**](#regions): Named parts, traversals, warps
6. [**Alignment**](#alignment): MatchClaims, AlignmentAnchors, MatchGraph, MatchLine, WarpMap, AlignmentBundle


## Foundations {#foundations}

### The timeline

A {{< glossary Timeline >}} is a positive coordinate axis minimally defined by
two properties:

- an **origin** (the zero coordinate), and
- a **measuring unit** that determines the type of timeline.

The measuring unit places each timeline in one of three **temporal domains**
(physical, logical, or graphical), each of which admits both continuous and
discrete representations. This yields six fundamental timeline types:

![The six timeline types. Each row corresponds to a temporal domain; each
column to a number type (continuous or discrete). The arrow convention is used
throughout: timelines are drawn as arrows progressing from left to
right.](figs/TTA_modelling-timelines.png){#fig-timeline-types}

| Domain | Modality | Continuous | Discrete |
|--------|----------|------------|----------|
| **Physical** | Hearing | seconds, milliseconds, minutes | samples |
| **Logical** | Conceptualising | quarter notes, beats | ticks, divisions |
| **Graphical** | Seeing | metres, centimetres, points | pixels |

: The six timeline types and their typical measuring units. {#tbl-timeline-types}

The physical domain captures acoustic time as experienced through hearing.
The logical domain captures symbolic musical time---the temporal structure
encoded in a score, independent of any particular performance or visual
rendering. The graphical domain captures spatial representations of time:
images, pages, and pixel coordinates.

A key observation: notation is *both* graphical and logical. A printed score
is, in effect, an alignment between a graphical timeline (pixel coordinates
on the page) and a logical timeline (quarter notes, beats, measures). This
duality is central to the model.

::: {.callout-note}
## On "temporal" in the graphical domain

Images are not themselves temporal objects. The graphical domain is called
"temporal" because graphical artefacts *encode* time spatially---a
spectromorphological analysis maps seconds to pixels, a score maps beats
to horizontal position. The timeline models this spatial encoding of time,
not a time dimension intrinsic to the image.

Video and animated scores straddle the physical and graphical domains: they
are physical renderings (at a frame rate, in seconds) of graphical content.
:::


### Coordinates and instants

::: {.definition}
::: {.definition-header}
Definition: Coordinate
:::
A **coordinate** represents a time-point in terms of its distance from the
timeline's origin as a positive real number associated with the timeline's
measuring unit.
:::

A coordinate is the model's most basic quantity: a scalar value paired with a
unit (e.g., 3.5 seconds, 480 ticks, 127 pixels). In the implementation, the
unit *determines* the number type rather than being declared beside it:
`quarters` and `beats` are exact fractions, discrete units (`ticks`,
`samples`, `frames`, `pixels`) are integers, and the remaining continuous
units are floats. That is what prevents silent rounding errors. Nothing is
quietly rounded to fit an axis: a value that cannot be expressed exactly on a
discrete axis raises rather than being nudged to the nearest integer, and
rounding happens only where a caller asks for it by name (`"round"`,
`"floor"`, `"ceil"`, `"truncate"`). The declared number type then survives
every boundary the value crosses, so a position read back from a fraction
axis is a fraction however it was computed.

::: {.definition}
::: {.definition-header}
Definition: Instant
:::
An **instant** associates a coordinate (a "time-point") with a signification
such as "start of event *e*."
:::

Everything a timeline accommodates is associated with a coordinate through
an Instant. Two Instants sharing an identical coordinate are **synchronous**
but not identical---the instant at which a note ends is ontologically separate
from the instant at which the next note begins, even when both share the same
coordinate.

::: {.visualisation}
::: {.vis-header}
Visualisation: Instant
:::
An Instant is represented as a **wedge** pointing at the timeline, labelled
with a coordinate value.
:::

Two principal sub-types are distinguished:

- **StartInstant**: marks the beginning of a {{< glossary TimeInterval >}}.
- **EndInstant**: marks the end of a TimeInterval.

Together, a StartInstant and an EndInstant define a **TimeInterval**: a
half-open interval [*s*, *e*) that is left-inclusive and right-exclusive.
This convention ensures that consecutive intervals (e.g., successive quarter
notes) tile the timeline without gaps or overlaps: the first quarter note
occupies [0, 1), the second [1, 2), and so on.

**Constraint**: The EndInstant's coordinate must be greater than or equal to
the corresponding StartInstant's coordinate.


### Events

::: {.definition}
::: {.definition-header}
Definition: Event
:::
We call anything associated with a timeline via an Instant or a TimeInterval
an **event**.
:::

This is a deliberately broad category. The model is agnostic to what events
represent---they may be notes, rests, annotations, audio segments, bounding
boxes, or any other entity that possesses a temporal location. Two principal
sub-types:

- **InstantEvent**: defined by a single Instant (zero duration).
- **TimeIntervalEvent**: defined by a StartInstant and an EndInstant
  (non-zero duration).

Events may carry arbitrary properties (pitch, dynamics, text labels, file
paths) that are relevant for querying and matching but are not part of the
temporal model itself.

![Events on a timeline. InstantEvents are marked by a single wedge;
TimeIntervalEvents span a region between two wedges (start and
end).](figs/TTA_modelling-instants.png){#fig-events}


### Basic operations

A timeline supports four basic operations:

1. **Addition**: inserting an Instant (and thereby its associated event).
2. **Removal**: deleting an Instant.
3. **Lookup**: retrieving all Instants at a given coordinate.
4. **Query**: retrieving all TimeIntervals spanning a given coordinate.

The **length** of a timeline is the distance between its origin and its last
coordinate with at least one Instant. A timeline may be **locked**, preventing
the addition of Instants beyond the last existing time-point.

### Synchrony

The model distinguishes two forms of synchrony:

- **Strict synchrony**: Instants sharing identical coordinates on the same
  timeline.
- **Pragmatic synchrony**: Instants binned together on the basis of a
  threshold (quantisation). Pragmatic synchrony is not yet implemented in the
  library but is planned as a configurable parameter.

Five default propositions govern Instants on a timeline:

1. Instants sharing the same coordinate are synchronous.
2. Temporally overlapping parts of TimeIntervals are strictly synchronous.
3. A later coordinate implies later occurrence *in that domain* (no
   cross-domain implication is entailed).
4. Every StartInstant necessitates a corresponding EndInstant, and vice versa.
5. An EndInstant's coordinate cannot be smaller than the corresponding
   StartInstant's.


## Flow Control {#flow-control}

### Contiguity

::: {.definition}
::: {.definition-header}
Definition: Contiguous TimeInterval
:::
A TimeInterval [*s*, *e*) is **contiguous** in the sense that it spans all
coordinates between its Start- and EndInstant monotonically. A TimeInterval
is said to **span** a coordinate *c* if *s* < *c* < *e*.
:::

::: {.definition}
::: {.definition-header}
Definition: Contiguous with
:::
We call **contiguous with TimeInterval [*s*, *e*)** all Instants synchronous
with *e*. By extension, any event located or starting at the end of a
TimeIntervalEvent is called contiguous with it.
:::

Contiguity is the default: a section of music flows into the next. Two
phenomena override this default.


### Breaks

::: {.definition}
::: {.definition-header}
Definition: Break
:::
A **break** is a control event that voids the contiguity at the Instant where
it is located.
:::

Events that would normally be contiguous at a break's coordinate become
discontiguous. Two constraints follow:

- A TimeInterval cannot be added if it would span a break's coordinate.
- A break cannot be placed at a coordinate already spanned by a TimeInterval.

Breaks encode phenomena such as the boundary between a *prima volta* and a
*seconda volta* ending, or the boundary at a *coda* sign where the default
sequential flow is interrupted.

::: {.visualisation}
::: {.vis-header}
Visualisation: Break
:::
Breaks are represented as **red lines orthogonal to the timeline axis**.
:::


### Jumps

::: {.definition}
::: {.definition-header}
Definition: Jump
:::
A **jump** is a control event defined by two Instants: a **JumpFrom** and a
**JumpTo** Instant. When active, it makes any event located or starting at
JumpTo contiguous with any event ending at JumpFrom.
:::

Jumps encode repeat signs, *dal segno al coda*, *da capo al fine*, and
analogous structures. Additional event properties define conditions under
which a control event is active (e.g., a *fine* is effective only after a
*da capo al fine*; *prima* and *seconda volta* brackets are conditionally
active depending on the traversal count).

::: {.visualisation}
::: {.vis-header}
Visualisation: Jump
:::
Jumps are represented as **dotted arrows** from the JumpFrom Instant to the
JumpTo Instant. The curvature of the arrow reflects the distance between the
two coordinates.
:::

Together, breaks and jumps form the **flow-control apparatus** of the model.
They determine how a timeline is traversed---which sections are played in what
order---without altering the underlying coordinate system. The traversal
itself is captured by a {{< glossary FlowMap >}} (see
[Derivative timelines](#derivative-timelines)).


## Conversion Maps {#conversion-maps}

::: {.definition}
::: {.definition-header}
Definition: ConversionMap (C-map)
:::
A **ConversionMap** is a typed function attached to a timeline that maps
each coordinate to exactly one value. If the function is bijective, we can
derive an **InverseMap**; also permits inverse conversion back to the
timeline's own unit.
:::

Conversion maps are at the heart of the model. They connect coordinate
systems, convert between units, and enable the transfer of information
across timelines.

::: {.visualisation}
::: {.vis-header}
Visualisation: ConversionMap
:::
Conversion maps are visualised as **double lines** adopting colour and
pattern from the type of timeline associated with the measuring unit that
they output (see @fig-cmaps). Maps outputting values other than coordinates
(e.g., string labels) use distinctly different colours or patterns.
:::

![Conversion maps map coordinates to other values, typically coordinates
in a different unit. The double-line convention distinguishes C-maps from
timelines.](figs/TTA_modelling-cmaps.png){#fig-cmaps}


### Output types

The output of a C-map can be:

- **A coordinate** in the same or a different unit (e.g., pixels to seconds,
  ticks to quarter notes). This is the most common case.
- **A specifier** such as a measure number, a filename, or a label.
- **An auxiliary constant** (e.g., a fixed y-coordinate for generating a
  horizontal line in an image).

When the output is a coordinate, the C-map implicitly defines a **derived
timeline** with variant coordinates. This is how a single DiscreteGraphicalTimeline
(pixels) can simultaneously express seconds, quarter notes, and *(x, y)* pairs.


### Bounded and unbounded maps

A C-map can be:

- **Unbounded**: applies globally across the entire timeline.
- **Bounded**: defines one or several **regions of vigour**
  ({{< glossary TimeInterval >}}s) within which it is valid. Outside these
  regions, the map returns no result.


### Map families

The implementation organises C-maps into families:

| Family | Description | Example |
|--------|-------------|---------|
| **Affine** (ScalarMultiplicationMap) | *y = ax + b* | pixels to seconds |
| **Lookup** (TableMap) | Explicit key-value mapping | tick to tempo |
| **Interpolation** | Linear interpolation between anchor points | warp path |
| **Constant** | Returns the same value for any input | y-coordinate of a staff line |
| **Straight line** | Generates *(x, y)* pairs for a line | horizontal system in an image |
| **Discretisation** | Rounds continuous to discrete | seconds to samples |
| **Periodic** (RotationMap) | Wraps coordinates cyclically | repeating ostinato |
| **Metric-aware** (FloorMap, MetricMap) | Beat and measure structure | quarters to measure number |

: Families of ConversionMaps in the `timetoalign` library. {#tbl-cmap-families}


### MultiMaps: composing conversion maps

Three composition strategies produce **MultiMaps**:

**CombinationMap**
:   Yields outputs from multiple C-maps simultaneously. For instance,
    combining an x-map and a y-map produces *(x, y)* coordinate pairs.

**ChainMap**
:   Applies C-maps in sequence: the output of one becomes the input of the
    next (e.g., ticks -> beats -> seconds). A ChainMap defines a **conversion
    path** and is a key building block for coordinate transfer.

**ConcatenationMap**
:   Combines bounded C-maps so that each coordinate region maps to one of
    them. For instance, a score with five systems has a ConcatenationMap of
    five StraightLineMaps, each valid within its system's pixel range.


## Nested Timelines {#nested-timelines}

A timeline can accommodate not only events but also other timelines.

### Children

::: {.definition}
::: {.definition-header}
Definition: Child
:::
A timeline is called a **Child** when it is recursively nested in a parent
timeline.
:::

A timeline can accommodate other timelines (Children) provided they use the
same measuring unit. Constraints mirror those for TimeIntervalEvents:

- A Child cannot span an existing {{< glossary Break >}} in the parent
  (unless explicitly adopted).
- Adding a Child may extend the parent's length only when the parent is not
  locked, and only within the parent's own parent's known length.
- Once added, a Child's length is **locked** by default to prevent side
  effects. An unlocked Child's length may change only within its parent's
  known length: a parent never grows because a Child grew.

Children introduce **relative coordinate systems** within a parent. A Child's
local origin is mapped to a specific coordinate of the parent; its local
coordinates are offsets from that origin. This is essential for modelling
multi-system score pages, where each system has its own pixel range but is
part of a single graphical timeline.

::: {.visualisation}
::: {.vis-header}
Visualisation: Child
:::
A Child is visualised as a timeline whose **EndInstant is marked by a hollow
diamond** (in contrast to the filled arrowhead of a root timeline).
:::

Children can overlap, leave gaps between them, carry their own C-maps, and
nest recursively to arbitrary depth.

![Nested timelines. The parent timeline contains two children (segments),
each with its own local coordinate system.](figs/TTA_modelling-Segments.png){#fig-segments}


### Segments and SegmentLines

::: {.definition}
::: {.definition-header}
Definition: Segment and SegmentLine
:::
When all Children of the same parent timeline ("siblings") are contiguous
with each other and tile the parent's full length, we call them **Segments**
and the parent a **SegmentLine**. A line is constructed as the runtime class
`SegmentLine[SegmentClass]`, for example
`SegmentLine[DiscreteGraphicalTimeline]`; nesting is expressed recursively as
`SegmentLine[SegmentLine[DiscreteGraphicalTimeline]]`. A line is also an
instance of its segment class and therefore exposes that class's full API.
:::

The key advantage of a SegmentLine is that contiguous siblings allow
**cumulative summing** of segment lengths and their C-maps (provided they
convert to the same unit relative to the segment's origin). This enables
efficient coordinate conversion across the entire structure. On any timeline,
`is_segment_line()` checks this structural tiling. `as_segment_line()` validates
the structure and homogeneous direct-child class before adopting the matching
parameterized class; `to_timeline()` drops segment enforcement, while
`to_typed()` re-types children recursively.

Four operations are associated with Children:

- **Addition**: adding a timeline as a Child, including all its events
  and C-maps.
- **Partitioning**: creating a new Child from a parent timeline and a
  TimeInterval.
- **Boundary-driven creation**: `create_children_from_boundaries()` creates
  *k* named, concrete Child timelines from *k*+1 coordinates. Boundaries
  spanning the full parent produce the structure accepted by
  `as_segment_line()`.
- **Concatenation**: `append_child(child, name=..., uid=...)` adds a Child at
  an unlocked parent's EndInstant and extends that parent. `add_child()`
  locks the timelines it embeds by default, so appending to one raises
  `RuntimeError`; nested structures are assembled from the inside out.

| Property | Region | Child | Segment |
|----------|--------|-------|---------|
| Is a timeline (holds events) | No | Yes | Yes |
| Siblings must be contiguous | No | No | Yes |
| Can span breaks | Yes | No | No |

: Comparison of Regions, Children, and Segments. {#tbl-children-comparison}


### TimeStamps

::: {.definition}
::: {.definition-header}
Definition: TimeStamp
:::
A **TimeStamp** is a set of values reflecting the coordinate of a root
timeline, the synchronous coordinates of all Children, and the conversion
results of all ConversionMaps associated respectively.
:::

A TimeStamp is a cross-section through a timeline hierarchy at a given
coordinate. It answers the question: "At coordinate *c* of the root
timeline, what are the local coordinates in each Child, and what do all
C-maps produce?"

By analogy, a **TimeIntervalStamp** combines a start TimeStamp and an end
TimeStamp, representing the cross-section of an interval through the
hierarchy.

::: {.visualisation}
::: {.vis-header}
Visualisation: TimeStamp
:::
TimeStamps are visualised as a **vertical cross-section** through a timeline
that intersects all Children and ConversionMaps at their synchronous points.
:::

![A timeline's internal data structures. The instants table records all
Instants with their coordinates, IDs, and types. The intervals table is
derived from the instants table and supports interval
queries.](figs/TTA_modelling-tables.png){#fig-tables}


## Regions and Derivative Timelines {#regions}

### Regions

A **Region** is a named part of a timeline defined by a
{{< glossary TimeInterval >}}. Regions are useful for referring to parts of
a timeline by name (e.g., "Chorus", "Verse", "Development") or by generic
labels (e.g., alphabetical letters for representing traversal paths).

Regions are *not* timelines: they do not accommodate events or C-maps.
They can, however, be used as the basis for **partitioning** a timeline into
Children---creating a Child whose boundaries correspond to the Region's
TimeInterval.


### Derivative Timelines {#derivative-timelines}

Three kinds of derived timelines play a central role in alignment:

**FlowMap**
:   A sequence of {{< glossary TimeInterval >}}s (often corresponding to
    previously defined {{< glossary Region >}}s) specifying a particular
    path through the timeline's control structure (repeats, jumps). A
    {{< glossary FlowMap >}} is computed from flow-control events
    ({{< glossary Break >}}s and {{< glossary Jump >}}s), or assembled directly
    from any interval descriptions---{{< glossary Region >}}s, coordinate pairs,
    {{< glossary Timeline >}}s, or interval events, given singly or as a
    collection. Its intervals can be partitioned and concatenated, **unfolding**
    the score into performance order: this materialises a new timeline of the
    source's own type whose played spans are appended as named children, each
    recorded as a {{< glossary Region >}} in performance coordinates.

    For example, a score with a repeat and a *dal segno al coda* has a
    FlowMap like [A, B, A, B, C, D] where some regions appear more than
    once. The unfolded timeline replays those spans as children in that order,
    a span played twice appearing as two children (the second suffixed
    `-rend2`, following the Verovio rendering-order convention).

**Converted timeline**
:   A timeline whose coordinates have been transformed to another unit via
    a {{< glossary ConversionMap >}} or {{< glossary ChainMap >}},
    potentially after applying a {{< glossary FlowMap >}}.

**WarpMap**
:   A derived timeline where coordinates have been re-adjusted to align with
    those of another timeline on the basis of
    {{< glossary AlignmentAnchor >}}s. See [Alignment](#alignment) for the
    full definition of WarpMap and the pipeline that produces it.


## Alignment {#alignment}

The alignment layer is where the model's cross-domain capability comes
together.

### MatchClaim

::: {.definition}
::: {.definition-header}
Definition: MatchClaim
:::
A **MatchClaim** is a claim of equivalence between events on different
timelines, with provenance metadata (agent, method, certainty). A MatchClaim
may be **synchronous** (producing {{< glossary AlignmentAnchor >}}s) or
**conceptual** (structural equivalence without temporal commitment). It may
include special **sentinel values** ({{< glossary NOMATCH >}}) explicitly
encoding the absence of a corresponding event on the other timeline.
:::

A MatchClaim takes the form of named references (IDs) of claimed-equivalent
events, combined with metadata on genesis:

- **Agent**: who or what produced the claim (human annotator, DTW algorithm,
  neural model, ...).
- **Decision criteria**: what evidence was used (temporal similarity,
  harmonic content, expert judgement, ...).
- **Certainty level**: how confident the agent is in the claim.

MatchClaims grow incrementally: an initial claim between events A and B can
be extended by adding B-C, creating a **match path** A -> B -> C that
connects three timelines. The model explicitly matches *events* (not
coordinates) to allow richer metadata about the alignment procedure.

Two levels of matching are distinguished:

- **Synchronous matching**: the matched events occupy corresponding temporal
  positions (e.g., "this beat in the score corresponds to this moment in
  the recording").
- **Conceptual matching**: the matched events are semantically equivalent
  but may not share a temporal correspondence (e.g., "both versions have
  a Bridge section, but they differ in length and internal structure").


### AlignmentAnchors

::: {.definition}
::: {.definition-header}
Definition: AlignmentAnchor
:::
An **AlignmentAnchor** is a pure coordinate pair associating one coordinate
on timeline A with one coordinate on timeline B. It is a neutral record
with no claim semantics---provenance and interpretation are carried by the
enclosing {{< glossary MatchClaim >}}. Only synchronous MatchClaims produce
AlignmentAnchors.
:::

From a {{< glossary MatchClaim >}} that associates
{{< glossary TimeIntervalEvent >}}s, two anchors are derived: a
**StartAnchor** and an **EndAnchor**. Based on the units present in the
aligned timelines, {{< glossary WarpMap >}}s can be constructed.

::: {.visualisation}
::: {.vis-header}
Visualisation: AlignmentAnchor
:::
AlignmentAnchors are visualised as **connecting lines** between TimeStamps,
using the same or a similar visual style as the Matches they derive from.
:::


#### MatchClaim cases

A MatchClaim always knows which pair of timelines it connects. It contains
0--2 {{< glossary AlignmentAnchor >}}s (only if synchronous), synchrony and
explicitness flags, and optional metadata (agent, decision criteria,
certainty). Four cases are distinguished:

1. **Event-to-event** (case a): two timed things on different timelines
   correspond---the core alignment operation.
2. **Projection** (case b): an event is projected onto a timeline with no
   matching event---useful for transferring annotations.
3. **NOMATCH** (case c): an event has no equivalent on the other
   timeline---a positive assertion of absence.
4. **Implicit** (case d): generated automatically by
   {{< glossary MatchGraph >}} group extension---e.g., when a match between
   two timelines implies coordinates on sibling timelines within the same
   {{< glossary TimelineGroup >}}.


### MatchGraph and MatchStamp

A **MatchGraph** is an on-demand analytical structure built from
MatchClaims. Nodes are `(timeline_id, coordinate)` tuples; edges derive
from the {{< glossary AlignmentAnchor >}}s of synchronous claims. Each
connected component yields a **MatchStamp**---a synchronised instant across
multiple timelines. A MatchGraph can be extended with implicit claims based
on {{< glossary TimelineGroup >}} membership. In the Hendrix example, each
Match box M1--M15 is a MatchGraph, not a single MatchClaim.

::: {.definition}
::: {.definition-header}
Definition: MatchStamp
:::
A **MatchStamp** is the union of {{< glossary TimeStamp >}}s from groups
synchronously connected by a {{< glossary MatchGraph >}}. It contains
one coordinate per participating timeline and, with `conversion_maps=True`,
the results of all {{< glossary ConversionMap >}}s associated with those
timelines. Unlike a {{< glossary TimeStamp >}}, where C-Map results are
visible by default, `conversion_maps` on every MatchStamp-producing getter
(`bundle.get_matchstamp_at()`, `get_matchstamps_at()`, `get_matchstamp_table()`,
`MatchClaim.get_matchstamp()`) is opt-in and defaults to `False`. This
differing default is a per-context parameter setting, not a break in stamp
uniformity: a MatchStamp exposes the identical `Stamp` interface ---
`get_coordinate_for()`, `get_coordinates_for()`, the `get_coordinate()`
dispatcher, `get_unit()`, `get_conversion_for()`, `present_timelines`,
`is_interpolated`, `to_dict()` --- as a `TimeStamp`, so a
stamp from any source keeps the same structure and behaviour regardless of
which keyword defaults were used to produce it.
:::

A MatchStamp from a single {{< glossary MatchClaim >}} contains the
TimeStamps for the claim's {{< glossary AlignmentAnchor >}}. A MatchStamp
from a MatchGraph contains *all* TimeStamps that the graph connects
through its connected components. Like a {{< glossary TimeStamp >}}, it
can be expanded with within-group coordinates (delegating to
{{< glossary TimelineGroup >}}) and, once opted in, C-map conversions.

`get_matchstamp_table()` extends the same opt-in flag to tabular output: with
`conversion_maps=True`, one derived column is added per timeline for each of
its enabled *numeric* unit-conversion maps (a map with a `target_unit`),
placed after the timeline columns. A label- or structure-valued conversion
map still surfaces in a MatchStamp's display but never becomes a table
column. A converted-unit column name that collides across timelines is
qualified as `"<timeline_id>:<unit>"`.


### The MatchLine

The **MatchLine** is an ordered sequence of {{< glossary AlignmentAnchor >}}s
derived from {{< glossary MatchClaim >}}s, sorted by coordinate on a source
timeline. It serves as input for {{< glossary WarpMap >}} generation.


### WarpMap

::: {.definition}
::: {.definition-header}
Definition: WarpMap
:::
A **WarpMap** is an interpolation-based coordinate mapping derived from
a {{< glossary MatchLine >}}; it enables non-linear coordinate transfer
between {{< glossary TimelineGroup >}}s.
:::

A WarpMap is generated from a MatchLine by extracting
`(source_coord, target_coord)` pairs and building an interpolation table.
If the source and target timelines have different units, the warped copy
is in the target's unit and of the appropriate timeline type (e.g., a
ContinuousLogicalTimeline warped to a ContinuousPhysicalTimeline). A
WarpMap requires at least two matching coordinate pairs for
interpolation. It is the mechanism by which non-linear temporal
correspondences---such as those between a rubato performance and a
metronomic score---are captured.


### AlignmentBundle {#alignment-bundle}

::: {.definition}
::: {.definition-header}
Definition: AlignmentBundle
:::
The **AlignmentBundle** is a collection of
{{< glossary TimelineGroup >}}s with inter-group
{{< glossary MatchClaim >}} connections; it provides coordinate transfer
via offset arithmetic, interpolation, and {{< glossary WarpMap >}}s.
:::

The AlignmentBundle provides coordinate transfer at two levels:

- **Within a group**: delegates to `TimelineGroup.get_timestamp_at()`,
  which converts linearly and exactly between members that share one start
  and one end.
- **Across groups**: constructs a {{< glossary MatchLine >}} from the
  cross-group claims, generates {{< glossary WarpMap >}}s on demand, and
  uses those WarpMaps for coordinate transfer.

The canonical user-facing query is `bundle.get_matchstamp_at(coord, tl_id)`,
which returns a {{< glossary MatchStamp >}} spanning all groups connected
to the queried timeline.

The full alignment object hierarchy, from atomic to composite, is:

```
AlignmentAnchor      (pure coordinate pair, no semantics)
    ↓
MatchClaim           (semantic claim about two timelines)
    ↓
MatchGraph           (on-demand graph from multiple claims)
    ↓
MatchStamp           (synchronised instant across N timelines)
    ↓
MatchLine            (ordered sequence of MatchStamps)
    ↓
WarpMap              (materialised timeline copy)
```


### Coordinate transfer {#coordinate-transfer}

The model implements three tiers of coordinate transfer:

1. **Offset arithmetic** for parent--child relationships: a child's
   coordinate is the parent's coordinate minus the child's offset.
   Exact and lossless.
2. **Interpolation** within {{< glossary TimelineGroup >}}s: members of
   potentially different units (e.g., seconds and samples) share one start
   and one end, so a position converts linearly and exactly, from each
   member's 0 and length.
3. **WarpMap** for cross-group alignment: derived from a
   {{< glossary MatchLine >}}, a WarpMap materialises a complete copy
   of a source timeline warped to a target timeline's coordinates.

Two timelines are **commensurable** if connected by a chain of C-maps,
membership in the same {{< glossary TimelineGroup >}}, or cross-group
{{< glossary MatchClaim >}}s. {{< glossary Commensurability >}} is the
precondition for coordinate transfer.

This layered architecture is what enables TimeToAlign! to propagate
annotations, transfer coordinates, and answer queries across arbitrarily
many representations of the same musical content---the central promise of
the model.


## Five Demonstration Scenarios

The TISMIR manuscript demonstrates the model through five worked examples
of increasing complexity. Each is accompanied by real-world data in the
specimen collection and (where applicable) a tutorial notebook.

| # | Scenario | Key concepts introduced | Specimen |
|---|----------|------------------------|----------|
| 1 | **SUPRA**: Aligning a historical piano roll with a digital score | Timeline (six types), C-map, Child, TimelineGroup, commensurability, TimeStamp | `specimens/supra_rolls/` |
| 2 | **Chorissimo**: Flow control in a school song with repeats | Segment, SegmentLine, Region, Break, Jump, FlowMap, RotationMap, unfolding | `specimens/audiolabs_omr/Chorissimo_Blue081/` |
| 3 | **Thoresen**: Transferring annotations between graphical analyses | MatchClaim, InverseMap, y-coordinate warping via custom C-map | `specimens/thoresen/` |
| 4 | **Beethoven**: Multimodal alignment across 23 timelines | FlowMap (unfolding at scale), AlignmentBundle, AlignmentAnchor, WarpMap, MatchLine | `specimens/beethoven_op18-4_iv/` |
| 5 | **Hendrix**: Studying the genesis of a rock song across three versions | MatchClaim (conceptual/synchronous), MatchGraph, NOMATCH, MatchStamp, certainty metadata | `specimens/hendrix/` |

: The five demonstration scenarios from the TISMIR manuscript. {#tbl-scenarios}
